nodes.name: Fourier dimension
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on $\mathbb{T}^d$. The Fourier dimension of $\mu$ is defined by \begin{equation} \dim_F(\mu)\coloneq \sup\big\{s\in [0,d):|\widehat{\mu}(\boldsymbol{n})|^2 = O(|\boldsymbol{n}|^{-s}) ~\text{as}~|\boldsymbol{n}|\to\infty\big\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of Fourier dimension
nodes.statement: \dim_F(\mu)\coloneq \sup\big\{s\in [0,d):|\widehat{\mu}(\boldsymbol{n})|^2 = O(|\boldsymbol{n}|^{-s}) ~\text{as}~|\boldsymbol{n}|\to\infty\big\}.
nodes.label: eq:def-Fourierdim

nodes.name: Positive part of logarithm log_+
nodes.statement: As usual, for all $x\in (0, \infty)$, we write $\log_+(x)=\max\{0,\log x\}$.

nodes.name: Exact Fourier dimension of GMC on the torus
nodes.statement: For any integer $d\ge 1$, there exists a centered log-correlated Gaussian field on $\mathbb{T}^d$ with covariance kernel \[ K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\log_+\frac{1}{d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})}+g(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus\{\boldsymbol{1}\}, \] where $g$ is a bounded continuous function on $\mathbb{T}^d$, such that for any $\gamma\in (0,\sqrt{2d})$, almost surely, the sub-critical GMC measure $\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma$ has Fourier dimension \[ \dim_F(\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma)= D_{\gamma,d}\coloneq \left\{ \begin{array}{cl} d-\gamma^2, & \text{if $0<\gamma<\sqrt{2d}/2$}, \vspace{2mm} \\ (\sqrt{2d}-\gamma)^2, & \text{if $\sqrt{2d}/2\leq\gamma<\sqrt{2d}$}. \end{array}\right. \]
nodes.statement_short: For every d there is a log-correlated field on T^d whose subcritical GMC has Fourier dimension D_{gamma,d} (d-gamma^2 or (sqrt(2d)-gamma)^2).
conclusions: there exists a centered log-correlated Gaussian field on $\mathbb{T}^d$ with covariance kernel
almost surely, the sub-critical GMC measure $\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma$ has Fourier dimension
nodes.label: thm:Fourier-decay-GMC

nodes.name: Torus versus unit cube: boundary effects
nodes.statement: We choose the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$ over the unit cube $[0,1)^d$ in \cite{LQT24,LQT25} to avoid boundary effects. A sharp truncation, for instance restricting a measure to the cube, changes its Fourier decay. For example, the Fourier coefficients of the Lebesgue measure on the cube decays as $|\boldsymbol{n}|^{-1}$ as $|\boldsymbol{n}|\to\infty$. This boundary effect may explain the lower bound restriction $\dim_F(\mu_\infty) \ge \min\{2, D_{\gamma,d}\}$ for the analysis on the cube in \cite[Theorem~1.2]{LQT25}. Indeed, if we replace the sharp cutoff with a smooth truncation function that is compactly supported in the interior of $(0,1)^d$, then the strategy in this paper could also be adapted to the unit cube. The torus, being free of boundaries, provides a more direct and natural setting for our analysis.
nodes.statement_short: The torus avoids boundary effects: a sharp truncation to the cube changes Fourier decay; a smooth cutoff would allow adapting the method to the cube.

nodes.name: Fourier dimension equals correlation dimension reformulation
nodes.statement: Recall that the correlation dimension of a measure $\mu$ is defined by (see, e.g.,~\cite[Lemma~2.6.6 and Definition~2.6.7]{BSS23}) \[ \dim_2(\mu)\coloneq \liminf_{\delta\to 0^+}\frac{\log \big(\sup\sum_i \mu(B(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\delta))^2\big)}{\log(1/\delta)}, \] where the supremum is taken over all family of disjoint balls. It is a known result that the correlation dimension is given by $D_{\gamma,d}$ (see, e.g.,~\cite[Theorem~3.1 and Formula(3.2)]{Ber23}, \cite[Section~4.2]{RV14} and \cite[Remark~2]{GV23}; see also \cite[Lemma~3.6]{LQT25} for a precise formulation): if the kernel \[ K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\log_+ \frac{1}{d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})}+g(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}) \] has bounded continuous remainder $g$, then for any $\gamma\in (0, \sqrt{2d})$, almost surely, \[ \dim_2(\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma)=D_{\gamma,d}. \] Therefore, we can reformulate Theorem~\ref{thm:Fourier-decay-GMC} by stating that there exists a log-correlated Gaussian field on $\mathbb{T}^d$, such that the corresponding sub-critical GMC measure has the same Fourier dimension as its correlation dimension.
nodes.statement_short: Recalls correlation dimension and the known result dim_2(GMC)=D_{gamma,d}, so Theorem 1.1 says Fourier and correlation dimensions coincide.

nodes.name: Correlation dimension
nodes.statement: Recall that the correlation dimension of a measure $\mu$ is defined by (see, e.g.,~\cite[Lemma~2.6.6 and Definition~2.6.7]{BSS23}) \[ \dim_2(\mu)\coloneq \liminf_{\delta\to 0^+}\frac{\log \big(\sup\sum_i \mu(B(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\delta))^2\big)}{\log(1/\delta)}, \] where the supremum is taken over all family of disjoint balls.

nodes.name: Correlation dimension of GMC
nodes.statement: It is a known result that the correlation dimension is given by $D_{\gamma,d}$ (see, e.g.,~\cite[Theorem~3.1 and Formula(3.2)]{Ber23}, \cite[Section~4.2]{RV14} and \cite[Remark~2]{GV23}; see also \cite[Lemma~3.6]{LQT25} for a precise formulation): if the kernel \[ K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\log_+ \frac{1}{d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})}+g(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}) \] has bounded continuous remainder $g$, then for any $\gamma\in (0, \sqrt{2d})$, almost surely, \[ \dim_2(\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma)=D_{\gamma,d}. \]
assumptions: the kernel \[ K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\log_+ \frac{1}{d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})}+g(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}) \] has bounded continuous remainder $g$
conclusions: \dim_2(\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma)=D_{\gamma,d}.

nodes.name: Log-correlated kernel on the torus
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})$ be a positive-definite kernel on $\mathbb{T}^d$ with \[ K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\log_+ \frac{1}{d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})}+g(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus \{\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{w}\}, \] where $g$ is a bounded function on $\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d$.

nodes.name: sigma-positive kernel
nodes.statement: Following Kahane~\cite{Kah85}, if $K$ can be decomposed as \begin{equation} K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\sum_{j=1}^\infty K_{j}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}), \end{equation} where $\mathcal{K}_j$ is continuous and non-negative definite kernel, then we say that $K$ is \textit{$\sigma$-positive}.

nodes.name: sigma-positivity decomposition
nodes.statement: K(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\sum_{j=1}^\infty K_{j}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}),
nodes.label: eq:sigma-positivity

nodes.name: Gaussian process psi_j generated by K_j
nodes.statement: Let $\psi_j$ be a centered Gaussian process generated by $K_j$.

nodes.name: Exponential processes X_j
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation} \Big\{X_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\exp\big(\gamma\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\frac{\gamma^2}{2}\mathbb{E}[\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})^2]\big):\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d\Big\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of X_j
nodes.statement: \Big\{X_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\exp\big(\gamma\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\frac{\gamma^2}{2}\mathbb{E}[\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})^2]\big):\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d\Big\}.
nodes.label: eq:def-Xj

nodes.name: Approximating measures mu_k
nodes.statement: Let \[ \mu_k(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq \prod_{j=1}^k X_j(\boldsymbol{z})\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}). \]

nodes.name: Kahane's T-martingale convergence
nodes.statement: According to Kahane's $T$-martingale theory~\cite{Kah87}, the sequence of random measures $\{\mu_k\}$ weakly converges to a limit random measure $\mu_{\infty}$ almost surely.

nodes.name: Non-degeneracy of subcritical GMC
nodes.statement: If $\gamma\in (0,\sqrt{2d})$, then the limit measure $\mu_\infty$ is non-degenerate, that is, $\mu_\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)\ne 0$, a.s.
conclusions: the limit measure $\mu_\infty$ is non-degenerate

nodes.name: Kahane's uniqueness: GMC independent of decomposition
nodes.statement: A key result from Kahane is that this limit measure is also independent of the decomposition in \eqref{eq:sigma-positivity}.

nodes.name: Gaussian multiplicative chaos measure GMC_K^gamma
nodes.statement: The GMC measure $\mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:Fourier-decay-GMC} is then defined by \[ \mathrm{GMC}_K^\gamma\coloneq \mu_\infty. \]

nodes.name: Fourier dimension bounded by correlation dimension
nodes.statement: The upper bound of $\dim_F(\mu_\infty)$ is given \[ \dim_F(\mu_\infty)\le \dim_2(\mu_\infty), \] while the exact value of correlation dimension $\dim_2(\mu_\infty)$ was known to be $D_{\gamma,d}$ (see Bertacco \cite[Theorem~3.1 and Formula~(3.2)]{Ber23}, Rhodes--Vargas \cite[Section~4.2]{RV14}, Garban--Vargas \cite[Remark~2]{GV23} and Lin--Qiu--Tan \cite[Lemma~3.6]{LQT25}).
nodes.statement_short: dim_F(mu_inf) <= dim_2(mu_inf), and dim_2(mu_inf)=D_{gamma,d} is known.

nodes.name: Space of Schwartz distributions on the torus
nodes.statement: Denote the space of Schwartz distributions on $\mathbb{T}^d$ by $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{T}^d)$.

nodes.name: Fourier--Lebesgue space
nodes.statement: Let $s\in \mathbb{R}$ and $1\le q<\infty$. The Fourier--Lebesgue space is defined as \[ \mathcal{F}L^{s,q}(\mathbb{T}^d)\coloneq \Big\{f\in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{T}^d):\|f\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{s,q}(\mathbb{T}^d)}<\infty\Big\}, \] with the norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{s,q}(\mathbb{T}^d)}$ defined by \begin{equation} \|f\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{s,q}(\mathbb{T}^d)}\coloneq \Big\{\sum_{\boldsymbol{n}\in \mathbb{Z}^d} \langle\boldsymbol{n}\rangle^{s q}|\widehat{f}(\boldsymbol{n})|^q\Big\}^{1/q},\quad 1\leq q<\infty, \end{equation} where \(\langle\boldsymbol{n}\rangle\coloneq (1+|\boldsymbol{n}|^2)^{1/2}\) and \[ |\boldsymbol{n}|\coloneq \Big(\sum_{i=1}^d |n_i|^2\Big)^{1/2},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{n}=(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_d)\in \mathbb{Z}^d. \]
nodes.statement_short: FL^{s,q}: distributions with finite weighted l^q norm of Fourier coefficients, weight <n>^{sq}.

nodes.name: Fourier--Lebesgue norm
nodes.statement: \|f\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{s,q}(\mathbb{T}^d)}\coloneq \Big\{\sum_{\boldsymbol{n}\in \mathbb{Z}^d} \langle\boldsymbol{n}\rangle^{s q}|\widehat{f}(\boldsymbol{n})|^q\Big\}^{1/q},\quad 1\leq q<\infty,
nodes.label: eq:def-FLnorm

nodes.name: Fourier--Lebesgue membership implies Fourier decay
nodes.statement: Note that once we can prove $f\in \mathcal{F}L^{s,q}$ for some $q\ge 1$, then we immediately have $|\widehat{f}(\boldsymbol{n})|=o(|\boldsymbol{n}|^{-s})$.
conclusions: $|\widehat{f}(\boldsymbol{n})|=o(|\boldsymbol{n}|^{-s})$

nodes.name: Fourier--Lebesgue spaces coincide with modulation and Wiener amalgam spaces
nodes.statement: It was shown in~\cite[Proposition~2.1 and Remark 4.2]{RSTT11} that the Fourier--Lebesgue space coincides with classical space like modulation space and Wiener amalgam space.

nodes.name: Uniform moment bound for Fourier--Lebesgue norm of GMC
nodes.statement: For any $\tau\in (0,D_{\gamma,d})$, there exist $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1<p\le 2\le q<\infty$, such that \[ \mathbb{E}\big[\|\mu_\infty\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{\tau/2,q}}^p\big]=\sup_{m\ge 1}\mathbb{E}\big[\|\mu_m\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{\tau/2,q}}^p\big]=\sup_{m\ge 1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\{\sum_{\boldsymbol{n}\in \mathbb{Z}^d} \langle\boldsymbol{n}\rangle^{\tau q/2}|\widehat{\mu}_m(\boldsymbol{n})|^q\Big\}^{p/q}\Big]<\infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: For tau < D_{gamma,d}, some p-th moment of the FL^{tau/2,q} norm of mu_m is bounded uniformly in m.
conclusions: there exist $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1<p\le 2\le q<\infty$, such that
nodes.label: prop:uniform-boundedness-Fourier-Lebesgue-norm

nodes.name: Vector-valued martingale method
nodes.statement: This method is called \textit{vector-valued martingale method}, which is initially introduced in~\cite{CHQW24} in the setting of Mandelbrot cascade and later applied on one-dimensional GMC measure in~\cite{LQT24} and several models including high dimensional GMC on $[0,1)^d$ in sequential work~\cite{LQT25}.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Random decoupling scheme: vector-valued martingale method

nodes.name: Decoupling into localized Fourier--Lebesgue norms
nodes.statement: Exploiting the inherent martingale structure of $\mu_m$ and applying Pisier's martingale type-$p$ inequality twice, we can decouple the $p$-moment of $\mathcal{F}L^{\tau/2,q}$ into sum of ``localized Fourier--Lebesgue norms'' of $\mu_m$, that is, \[ \mathbb{E}\big[\|\mu_m\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{\tau/2,q}}^p\big]\lesssim \sum_{k=1}^m \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathscr{D}_k}\mathbb{E}[\|\mathfrak{D}_{\boldsymbol{I}}^\varphi\|_{\ell^q}^p], \] where \begin{equation} \mathfrak{D}_{\boldsymbol{I}}^\varphi(\boldsymbol{n})\coloneq \langle \boldsymbol{n}\rangle^{\tau/2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}(\boldsymbol{z})\bigg[\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}X_j(\boldsymbol{z})\bigg]\cdot(X_k(\boldsymbol{z})-1)\cdot \boldsymbol{z}^{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}) \end{equation} and the support of $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}$ is concentrated in a small neighbourhood of $\boldsymbol{I}$ (see \S\ref{sssec:pou} for its precise statement).
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Random decoupling scheme: vector-valued martingale method
nodes.statement_short: Two applications of Pisier's inequality bound E||mu_m||^p by a sum over scales and dyadic cubes of localized norms ||D_I^phi||.
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\big[\|\mu_m\|_{\mathcal{F}L^{\tau/2,q}}^p\big]\lesssim \sum_{k=1}^m \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathscr{D}_k}\mathbb{E}[\|\mathfrak{D}_{\boldsymbol{I}}^\varphi\|_{\ell^q}^p],

nodes.name: Localized Fourier coefficient D_I^phi
nodes.statement: \mathfrak{D}_{\boldsymbol{I}}^\varphi(\boldsymbol{n})\coloneq \langle \boldsymbol{n}\rangle^{\tau/2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}(\boldsymbol{z})\bigg[\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}X_j(\boldsymbol{z})\bigg]\cdot(X_k(\boldsymbol{z})-1)\cdot \boldsymbol{z}^{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Random decoupling scheme: vector-valued martingale method
nodes.label: eq:intro-def-DIphi

nodes.name: Spectral leakage of sharp versus smooth windows
nodes.statement: This can be seen even in the simplest deterministic case. Consider the constant function $f(z) = 1$ for all $z \in \mathbb{T}\coloneq\{z\in \mathbb{C}:|z|=1\}$. Its Fourier series is trivial, with coefficients $\widehat{f}(0) = 1$ and $\widehat{f}(n) = 0$ for all $n \neq 0$. This represents a perfect spectrum with no leakage. Now, let's observe the effect of applying a window function to $f(z)$. We compare two cases: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{A sharp window:} Let $g_1(z)$ be the characteristic function of the arc $\{e^{2\pi i t}:t\in [-1/4, 1/4]\}$. To compute its $n$-th Fourier coefficient, we use the parameterization $z=e^{2\pi it}$: \[ \widehat{f\cdot g_1}(n) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} g_1(z) z^n\,m(\mathrm{d}z) = \int_{-1/4}^{1/4} e^{2\pi i nt}\,\mathrm{d}t = \frac{\sin(\pi n/2)}{\pi n}. \] This exhibits a slow algebraic decay of order $|n|^{-1}$ as $|n|\to \infty$, which is a poor approximation of the true spectrum (which is zero). \item \textbf{A smooth window:} Let $g_2(z)$ be any $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb{T}$ supported on the same arc. Its $n$-th Fourier coefficient is \[ \widehat{f\cdot g_2}(n) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} g_2(z) z^n\,m(\mathrm{d}z)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}g(e^{it})e^{2\pi i nt}\,\mathrm{d}t. \] Through repeated integration by parts, we can see that its coefficients decay faster than any polynomial, that is, $|\widehat{g_2}(n)| = O(|n|^{-k})$ as $|n|\to \infty$ for any $k \in \mathbb{N}$. \end{enumerate} The rapid decay of $\widehat{g_2}(n)$ is a far better approximation of the zero-valued spectrum of the original signal $f(z)=1$. This illustrates how a smooth window better preserves the underlying spectral properties.
nodes.statement_short: Sharp window on T gives |n|^{-1} Fourier decay; smooth window gives faster-than-polynomial decay.

nodes.name: d-dimensional torus
nodes.statement: Let $d\ge 1$ be an integer. We identify $d$-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^d$ with $(S^1)^d\subset \mathbb{C}^d$ by \[ \mathbb{T}^d\coloneq\{(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_d)\in \mathbb{C}^d:|z_i|=1,i=1,2,\ldots,d\}. \]

nodes.name: Group operation on the torus
nodes.statement: The group operation on $\mathbb{T}^d$ is coordinate-wise multiplication, that is, for $\boldsymbol{z}=(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_d)$ and $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_d)$ in $\mathbb{T}^d$, \[ \boldsymbol{z}\cdot \boldsymbol{w}\coloneq (z_1w_1,z_2w_2,\ldots,z_d w_d). \]

nodes.name: Juxtaposition notation for torus product
nodes.statement: We also write $\boldsymbol{z}\boldsymbol{w}$ instead of $\boldsymbol{z}\cdot \boldsymbol{w}$ for simplicity.

nodes.name: Unit of the torus
nodes.statement: The unit of multiplication on $\mathbb{T}^d$ is denoted by $\boldsymbol{1}$.

nodes.name: Exponential e(t)
nodes.statement: As usual, we denote \[ e(t)=e^{2\pi i t},\quad \forall t\in \mathbb{R}. \]

nodes.name: Parametrization map E
nodes.statement: For convenience, we define \begin{align*} \begin{array}{cccc} \mathcal{E}\colon & \mathbb{R}^d& \xrightarrow{\quad\quad} & \mathbb{T}^d \vspace{2mm} \\ & (t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d) & \mapsto& (e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d)). \end{array} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Parametrization of the torus
nodes.statement: \mathbb{T}^d=\big\{\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t})\in \mathbb{C}^d:\boldsymbol{t}\in [-1/2,1/2)^d\big\}.
nodes.label: Td-para

nodes.name: Torus norm
nodes.statement: For each point $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$, define \[ \|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d}\coloneq \inf_{\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t})=\boldsymbol{z}}\|\boldsymbol{t}\|, \] where $\|\boldsymbol{t}\|$ is the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^d$, that is, \[ \|\boldsymbol{t}\|=\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^d |t_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in \mathbb{R}^d. \]

nodes.name: Standard metric on the torus
nodes.statement: This induces the metric $d_{\mathbb{T}^d}$ on $\mathbb{T}^d$ by \begin{equation} d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})\coloneq\|\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d, \end{equation} where $\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}=(\bar{w}_1,\bar{w}_2,\ldots,\bar{w}_d)$ is the complex conjugate of $\boldsymbol{w}$.

nodes.name: Torus distance
nodes.statement: d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})\coloneq\|\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d,
nodes.label: eq:def-distance-Td

nodes.name: Closed ball on the torus
nodes.statement: For $r>1$ and $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$, we denote \[ \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},r)\coloneq \{\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d:d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})\le r\}. \]

nodes.name: Closed ball in R^d
nodes.statement: While we reserve the symbol $\overline{B}(\boldsymbol{t},r)$ for closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, that is, \[ \overline{B}(\boldsymbol{t},r)\coloneq\{\boldsymbol{s}\in \mathbb{R}^d:\|\boldsymbol{t}-\boldsymbol{s}\|\le r\}. \]

nodes.name: Dyadic cubes of generation j
nodes.statement: Denote the family of $j$-th generation of dyadic cubes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ by \[ \widetilde{\mathscr{D}}_{j}^d=\widetilde{\mathscr{D}}_{j}\coloneq \bigg\{[0,2^{-j})^d+2^{-j}\boldsymbol{h}: \boldsymbol{h}\in \mathbb{Z}^d\bigg\} \] and the family of $j$-th generation of dyadic cubes in $[-1/2,1/2)^d$, that is, the Euclidean coordinate of $\mathbb{T}^d$, by \begin{equation} \mathscr{D}_{j}^d=\mathscr{D}_{j}\coloneq \bigg\{[0,2^{-j})^d+2^{-j}\boldsymbol{h}: \boldsymbol{h}\in \big\{-2^j,-2^j+1,\ldots,2^{j}-1\big\}^d\bigg\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dyadic cubes in [-1/2,1/2)^d
nodes.statement: \mathscr{D}_{j}^d=\mathscr{D}_{j}\coloneq \bigg\{[0,2^{-j})^d+2^{-j}\boldsymbol{h}: \boldsymbol{h}\in \big\{-2^j,-2^j+1,\ldots,2^{j}-1\big\}^d\bigg\}.
nodes.label: eq:def-D_j

nodes.name: Scaled concentric cube
nodes.statement: For any cube $\boldsymbol{I} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and scalar $\lambda > 0$, we denote by $\lambda \boldsymbol{I}$ the cube concentric with $\boldsymbol{I}$ and scaled by a factor of $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Length of a multi-index
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol{\alpha}= (\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in \mathbb{N}^d$ be a multi-index. The length $|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|$ of $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is defined by \[ |\boldsymbol{\alpha}|\coloneq \alpha_1+\alpha_2+\cdots+\alpha_d. \]

nodes.name: Partial derivatives on the torus
nodes.statement: For any sufficiently smooth function $f\colon \mathbb{T}^d\to \mathbb{C}$ written as \[ (e(t_1),e(t_2), \ldots, e(t_d))\mapsto f(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d)) \] and any multi-index $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_d)$, define \[ (D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} f)(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\coloneq (D_1^{\alpha_1}D_2^{\alpha_2}\cdots D_d^{\alpha_d}f)(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d)), \] where $D_i$ denotes the first order partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $t_i$, that is, \[ (D_i f)(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\coloneq\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(e(t_1),\ldots,e(t_i+h),\ldots,e(t_d))-f(e(t_1),\ldots,e(t_i),\ldots,e(t_d))}{h}. \]

nodes.name: Partial derivatives on R^d
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $g \colon U\to \mathbb{R},\boldsymbol{t}\mapsto g (\boldsymbol{t})$ is a sufficient smooth function on a domain $U\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, to distinguish from the partial derivatives on $\mathbb{T}^d$, we denote the partial derivative of $g$ with respect to the $i$-th coordinate by $\partial_i g$ and \[ (\partial^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} g)(\boldsymbol{t})\coloneq (\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\partial_2^{\alpha_2}\cdots \partial_d^{\alpha_d}g)(\boldsymbol{t}). \]

nodes.name: Normalized Haar measure on the torus
nodes.statement: We also denote by $\boldsymbol{m}$ the normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb{T}^d$. To be specific, for any $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$, \begin{align*} \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} f(\boldsymbol{z})\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})&=\int_{[-1/2,1/2)^d}f(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\,\mathrm{d}t_1\mathrm{d}t_2\cdots\mathrm{d}t_d \\ & =\int_{[-1/2,1/2)^d}f(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}))\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}, \end{align*} where $\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}\coloneq \mathrm{d}t_1\mathrm{d}t_2\cdots\mathrm{d}t_d$ is the Lebesgue measure on $[-1/2,1/2)^d$.

nodes.name: C^k norm
nodes.statement: For any integer $k \ge 1$ and any $C^k(\mathbb{R}^d)$ function $f$, its $C^k$-norm is defined by \[ \|f\|_{C^k(\mathbb{R}^d)}\coloneq \sum_{|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|\le k}\|\partial^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}f\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)}. \]

nodes.name: Characters e_n
nodes.statement: We also use the standard notation \[ e_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{t})\coloneq e\bigg(\sum_{\ell=1}^d n_\ell t_\ell\bigg),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in \mathbb{R}^d \text{\, and \,} \boldsymbol{n}\in \mathbb{Z}^d. \]

nodes.name: Fourier transform on the torus (without conjugate)
nodes.statement: The Fourier transform of a function $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$ is defined by\footnote{We remind the reader that our definition of the Fourier transform differs slightly from the conventional one, in which $\widehat{f}(\boldsymbol{n})=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} f(\boldsymbol{z})\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}^{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})$. We choose this different convention omitting the complex conjugate for simplicity of notation.} \[ \widehat{f}(\boldsymbol{n})\coloneq \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} f(\boldsymbol{z})\boldsymbol{z}^{\boldsymbol{n}}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})=\int_{[-1/2,1/2)^d}f(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}))e_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{t})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{n}\in \mathbb{Z}^d. \]
nodes.statement_short: Fourier coefficient hat f(n) = integral of f(z) z^n dm, a convention omitting the complex conjugate.

nodes.name: Differentiation of convolutions
nodes.statement: Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$ and $P\in C^k(\mathbb{T}^d)$ for some $k\in \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$. Then the convolution of $f$ and $P$ \[ (P*f)(\boldsymbol{z})=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}})f(\boldsymbol{w})\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z} \in \mathbb{T}^d \] is a $C^k$-function and for any multi-index $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ with $|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|\le k$, we have \begin{equation} D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(P*f)(\boldsymbol{z})=((D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P)*f)(\boldsymbol{z}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \end{equation}
conclusions: is a $C^k$-function
for any multi-index $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ with $|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|\le k$, we have
nodes.label: lemma:convolution-deterministic

nodes.name: Derivative of convolution
nodes.statement: D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(P*f)(\boldsymbol{z})=((D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P)*f)(\boldsymbol{z}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d.
nodes.label: eq:diff-convolution

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: The proof of $\mathbb{R}^d$ version can be found in~\cite[Proposition~4.20]{Bre11}. The same proof applies verbatim to $\mathbb{T}^d$, since the argument relies only on local properties.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the R^d version (Brezis) and note the argument is local, so it transfers to T^d.

nodes.name: Mollification of Gaussian processes
nodes.statement: Let $(\xi(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ be a Gaussian process with continuous paths almost surely. For any $k\in \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ and $P\in C^k(\mathbb{T}^d)$, define \[ \psi(\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq (P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{z})=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{w})\xi(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}})\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \] Then the Gaussian process $(\psi(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ has $C^k$-paths almost surely and its covariance kernel is given by \[ \mathbb{E}[\psi(\boldsymbol{z}_1)\psi(\boldsymbol{z}_2)]=\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P(\boldsymbol{w}_2)\mathbb{E}\big[\xi(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\xi(\boldsymbol{z}_2\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\big]\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2). \]
nodes.statement_short: Convolving a continuous Gaussian process with a C^k kernel gives a Gaussian process with C^k paths and an explicit covariance.
assumptions: $(\xi(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ be a Gaussian process with continuous paths almost surely
conclusions: the Gaussian process $(\psi(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ has $C^k$-paths almost surely and its covariance kernel is given by
nodes.label: lemma:mollification-Gaussian-process

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $((P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ is a Gaussian process. Let $\boldsymbol{z}_1,\boldsymbol{z}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{z}_n\in \mathbb{T}^d$ and we shall show that \[ \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k (P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{z}_k)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{w})\cdot \bigg(\sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \xi(\boldsymbol{z}_k\bar{\boldsymbol{w}} )\bigg)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}) \] is still a Gaussian random variable for any $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_n\in \mathbb{R}$. But now, $(\sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \xi(\boldsymbol{z}_k\boldsymbol{w}))_{\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ forms a new continuous Gaussian process on $\mathbb{T}^d$. Therefore, it is sufficient to prove that $(P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{1})$ is Gaussian. Let $\mathcal{P}_n$ be a partition of $[-1/2,1/2)^d$ into cubes of side length $1/n$. For each $\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathcal{P}_n$, we arbitrary pick a point $\boldsymbol{w}_{\boldsymbol{I}}\in \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{I})$. Denote the volume of $\boldsymbol{I}$ in Lebesgue measure by $\operatorname{Vol}(\boldsymbol{I})$. Then the Riemann sum \[ \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathcal{P}_n} P(\boldsymbol{w}_{\boldsymbol{I}})\xi(\boldsymbol{1}\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\boldsymbol{I}})\cdot \operatorname{Vol}(\boldsymbol{I})=n^{-d}\sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathcal{P}_n} P(\boldsymbol{w}_{\boldsymbol{I}})\xi(\boldsymbol{1}\cdot\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\boldsymbol{I}}) \] converges to $(P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{1})$ as $n\to \infty$. Since $\xi(\boldsymbol{z})$ is a Gaussian process, the Riemann sum is a Gaussian random variables. Therefore, the limit random variable $(P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{1})$ is Gaussian.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce Gaussianity of finite linear combinations to (P*xi)(1), then approximate by Riemann sums of Gaussians.

nodes.name: Reduce to showing P*xi is a Gaussian process
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $((P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ is a Gaussian process.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing P*xi is a Gaussian process

nodes.name: Take finite linear combinations of P*xi at points
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol{z}_1,\boldsymbol{z}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{z}_n\in \mathbb{T}^d$ and we shall show that \[ \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k (P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{z}_k)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{w})\cdot \bigg(\sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \xi(\boldsymbol{z}_k\bar{\boldsymbol{w}} )\bigg)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}) \] is still a Gaussian random variable for any $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_n\in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take finite linear combinations of P*xi at points

nodes.name: Reduce to Gaussianity of (P*xi)(1)
nodes.statement: But now, $(\sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \xi(\boldsymbol{z}_k\boldsymbol{w}))_{\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ forms a new continuous Gaussian process on $\mathbb{T}^d$. Therefore, it is sufficient to prove that $(P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{1})$ is Gaussian.

nodes.name: Introduce cube partitions and sample points
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}_n$ be a partition of $[-1/2,1/2)^d$ into cubes of side length $1/n$. For each $\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathcal{P}_n$, we arbitrary pick a point $\boldsymbol{w}_{\boldsymbol{I}}\in \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{I})$. Denote the volume of $\boldsymbol{I}$ in Lebesgue measure by $\operatorname{Vol}(\boldsymbol{I})$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce cube partitions and sample points

nodes.name: Riemann sums converge to (P*xi)(1)
nodes.statement: Then the Riemann sum \[ \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathcal{P}_n} P(\boldsymbol{w}_{\boldsymbol{I}})\xi(\boldsymbol{1}\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\boldsymbol{I}})\cdot \operatorname{Vol}(\boldsymbol{I})=n^{-d}\sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathcal{P}_n} P(\boldsymbol{w}_{\boldsymbol{I}})\xi(\boldsymbol{1}\cdot\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\boldsymbol{I}}) \] converges to $(P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{1})$ as $n\to \infty$.

nodes.name: Limit of Gaussians is Gaussian
nodes.statement: Since $\xi(\boldsymbol{z})$ is a Gaussian process, the Riemann sum is a Gaussian random variables. Therefore, the limit random variable $(P*\xi)(\boldsymbol{1})$ is Gaussian.

nodes.name: Pisier's martingale type inequality
nodes.statement: We shall use the following well-known fact in the theory of Banach space geometry (see~\cite[Proposition~10.36 and Definition~10.41]{Pis16}): \begin{center} {\it For any $2\le q<\infty$, the Banach space $\ell^q$ has martingale type $p$ for all $1<p\le 2$. } \end{center} More precisely, for any $1<p\le 2\le q<\infty$, there exists a constant $C(p, q)>0$ such that any $\ell^q$-vector-valued martingale $(F_m)_{m\ge 0}$ in $L^p(\mathbb{P}; \ell^q)$ satisfies \begin{align} \mathbb{E} [\| F_m\|_{\ell^q}^p] \le C(p,q) \sum_{k=0}^m \mathbb{E}[\|F_k- F_{k-1}\|_{\ell^q}^p], \end{align} with the convention $F_{-1}\equiv 0$.
nodes.statement_short: For 1<p<=2<=q, l^q has martingale type p: E||F_m||^p <= C sum of E||increments||^p.
conclusions: the Banach space $\ell^q$ has martingale type $p$ for all $1<p\le 2$

nodes.name: Martingale type p inequality
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E} [\| F_m\|_{\ell^q}^p] \le C(p,q) \sum_{k=0}^m \mathbb{E}[\|F_k- F_{k-1}\|_{\ell^q}^p],
nodes.label: eq:def-Mtype

nodes.name: Type-p inequality for independent centered l^q variables
nodes.statement: The inequality \eqref{eq:def-Mtype} implies in particular that for any family of independent and centered $\ell^q$-valued random variables $(G_k)_{k=0}^m$ in $L^p(\mathbb{P}; \ell^q)$, \begin{align} \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\|\sum_{k=0}^m G_k\Big\|_{\ell^q}^p\Big] \le C(p,q)\sum_{k =0}^m \mathbb{E}[\|G_k \|_{\ell^q}^p]. \end{align}
assumptions: any family of independent and  centered  $\ell^q$-valued random variables $(G_k)_{k=0}^m$  in $L^p(\mathbb{P}; \ell^q)$

nodes.name: Type-p inequality for independent sums
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\|\sum_{k=0}^m G_k\Big\|_{\ell^q}^p\Big] \le C(p,q)\sum_{k =0}^m \mathbb{E}[\|G_k \|_{\ell^q}^p].
nodes.label: eq:def-ind-Mtype

nodes.name: Burkholder's martingale inequality
nodes.statement: For further reference, note that when $1<p\le 2$, if $(T_m)_{m\ge 0}$ is a scalar martingale, the inequality \eqref{eq:def-Mtype} follows from the classical Burkholder's martingale inequality and reads as \[ \mathbb{E}[|T_m|^p]\le C(p)\sum_{k=0}^m\mathbb{E}[|T_k-T_{k-1}|^p], \] with the convention $T_{-1}\equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Scalar type-p inequality for independent centered variables
nodes.statement: Moreover, the inequality \eqref{eq:def-ind-Mtype} implies that for any family of independent and centered random variables $(Y_k)_{k=0}^m$ in $L^p(\mathbb{P})$, \begin{align} \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big|\sum_{k=0}^m Y_k \Big|^p\Big]\le C(p)\sum_{k=0}^m \mathbb{E}[|Y_k|^p]. \end{align}
assumptions: any family of independent and  centered random variables $(Y_k)_{k=0}^m$  in $L^p(\mathbb{P})$

nodes.name: Scalar inequality for independent sums
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big|\sum_{k=0}^m Y_k \Big|^p\Big]\le C(p)\sum_{k=0}^m \mathbb{E}[|Y_k|^p].
nodes.label: eq:def-ind-Mtype-scalar

nodes.name: Smooth partition of unity on T^d
nodes.statement: Let $d\ge 1$ be an integer. There exists a sequence of $C^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)$-functions $\{\varphi_k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}}$ such that for any $k\ge 1$, the following properties hold: \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] The translations of $\varphi_k$ form a partition of unity on $\mathbb{T}^d$, that is, \begin{equation} \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathscr{D}_k} \varphi_{k}(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}-\boldsymbol{c_I}))=1,\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}\in [-1/2,1/2)^d. \end{equation} \item[(2)] The support of $\varphi_k$ is contained in $\mathcal{E}([-2^{-k},2^{k}]^d)\coloneq \{\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}):\boldsymbol{t}\in [-2^{-k},2^{k}]^d \}$. \item[(3)] For each $\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in \mathbb{N}^d$, the derivatives of $\varphi_k$ satisfy the scaling property \[ \|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \varphi_k\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}\le C(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|) 2^{k|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|}, \] where the constant $C(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|)$ is independent of $k$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Dyadic-scale smooth partitions of unity on T^d with supports of size 2^{-k} and derivative bounds C 2^{k|alpha|}.
conclusions: There exists a sequence of $C^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)$-functions $\{\varphi_k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}}$ such that for any $k\ge 1$, the following properties hold:
nodes.label: lemma:pou-scaling-Td

nodes.name: Partition of unity identity
nodes.statement: \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathscr{D}_k} \varphi_{k}(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}-\boldsymbol{c_I}))=1,\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}\in [-1/2,1/2)^d.
nodes.label: eq:pou-Td-euclidean-coordinate

nodes.name: Translated window functions phi_I
nodes.statement: Define $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}))\coloneq\varphi_k(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}-\boldsymbol{c_I}))$ for each $\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathscr{D}_k$.

nodes.name: phi_I form a partition of unity supported in E(2I)
nodes.statement: Then \eqref{eq:pou-Td-euclidean-coordinate} can be rewritten as \[ \sum_{\boldsymbol{I}\in \mathscr{D}_k} \varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}(\boldsymbol{t})=1,\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}\in \mathbb{T}^d, \] and the support of $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}$ \[ \operatorname{supp} \varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}\subset \mathcal{E}(2\boldsymbol{I})\coloneq \{\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}):\boldsymbol{t}\in 2\boldsymbol{I}\}. \]

nodes.name: Translation invariance of derivatives of phi_I
nodes.statement: Since \[ [D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\varphi_k(\mathcal{E}(\cdot-\boldsymbol{s}))](\boldsymbol{t})=(D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\varphi_k)(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}-\boldsymbol{s})),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{s}\in \mathbb{T}^d, \] we have $\|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}=\|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives commute with translation, so phi_I has the same sup norms of derivatives as phi_k.

nodes.name: Derivative scaling of phi_I
nodes.statement: Hence the scaling property of the derivatives of $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}$ is also satisfied, that is, \[ \|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \varphi_{\boldsymbol{I}}\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}\le C(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|) 2^{k|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|}. \]

nodes.statement: Let $(\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ be a sequence of stationary, centered Gaussian processes, indexed by $j=1, 2, \ldots$.

nodes.name: Covariance kernel K_j
nodes.statement: We define their covariance kernel as \[ K_j(\boldsymbol{z}, \boldsymbol{w}) \coloneq \mathbb{E}[\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}) \psi_j(\boldsymbol{w})]. \]

nodes.name: One-variable kernel function mathcal K_j

nodes.name: Log-correlated Gaussian field with smooth decomposition
nodes.statement: There exists a sequence of independent, stationary, centered Gaussian processes, denoted by $(\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z} \in \mathbb{T}^d}$ for each $j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$, whose associated covariance kernels $\mathcal{K}_j$ and functions $K_j$ (as defined above) satisfy the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(P0)] (Smoothness). The sample paths of all the Gaussian processes $(\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$ belong to $C^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)$ almost surely. \item[(P1)] (Finite dependence). If $d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z}, \boldsymbol{w}) \ge 3 \cdot 2^{-j}$, then the kernel $K_j(\boldsymbol{z}, \boldsymbol{w}) = 0$. \item[(P2)] (Sum to log-correlation). The sum of the covariance kernels is of logarithmic type: \[ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} K_j(\boldsymbol{z}, \boldsymbol{w}) = \log_+ \frac{1}{d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z}, \boldsymbol{w})} + g(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}), \quad \text{with $g \in C(\mathbb{T}^d)$.} \] \item[(P3)] (Limiting variance). The variances of the processes, given by $\mathcal{K}_j(\mathbf{1})$, have the limit: \[ \lim_{j \to \infty} \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{1}) =\lim\limits_{j\to \infty}\mathbb{E}[\psi_j(\boldsymbol{t})^2]=\log 2. \] \item[(P4)] (Uniform Derivative Bounds). There exists an increasing function $\Theta: (0, \infty) \to [1, \infty)$ such that for all $p > 0$, \begin{align} \sup_{j} \sup_{|\boldsymbol{\alpha}| \le d} \sup_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d} \frac{\mathbb{E}[|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^p]}{j^{2|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}2^{j|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}} \le \Theta(p). \end{align} \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Existence of log-correlated Gaussian field with smooth decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Existence of independent stationary smooth Gaussian processes psi_j with finite range 3*2^{-j}, covariances summing to log-correlation, variance -> log 2, and derivative moment bounds.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of Theta is no restriction
nodes.statement: The increasing condition on the function $\Theta$ in \eqref{incr-p-moment} will be convenient for us later. We may only assume that $\Theta(p)<\infty$ for all $p>0$ and drop the increasing condition. Indeed, if \[ \widetilde{\Theta}(p): = \sup_{j} \sup_{|\boldsymbol{\alpha}| \le d} \sup_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d} \frac{\mathbb{E}[|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^p]}{j^{2|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}2^{j|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}} <\infty \quad \text{for all $p>0$}, \] then by noting that $ p\mapsto (\mathbb{E}[|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^p]/ (j^{2|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}2^{j|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}))^{1/p} $ is increasing on $p$, we may obtain an increasing function $\Theta$ satisfying \eqref{incr-p-moment} by setting \[ \Theta(p)= \sup_{0<q\le p} \widetilde{\Theta}(q)<\infty. \]

nodes.name: Periodization of compactly supported positive definite functions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a positive definite function on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\operatorname{supp} \mathcal{L}\subset [-1/2,1/2]^d$. Define \[ \mathcal{H}(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}))\coloneq \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{t}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}\in [-1/2,1/2)^d. \] Then $\mathcal{H}$ is a positive definite function on $\mathbb{T}^d$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: We will use $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{T}^d}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}^d}$ to distinguish Fourier transforms on $\mathbb{T}^d$ and $\mathbb{R}^d$ for the moment. Since $\mathcal{L}$ is positive definite on $\mathbb{R}^d$, we have $(\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\mathcal{L})(\boldsymbol{\xi})\ge 0$ for all $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^d$. By definition, for any $\boldsymbol{n}=(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_d)\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, we have \begin{align*} (\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{T}^d}\mathcal{H})(\boldsymbol{n})&=\int_{[-1/2,1/2)^d}\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{t}))e_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{t})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}\\ &=\int_{[-1/2,1/2)^d}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{t})e_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{t})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}=(\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\mathcal{L})(\boldsymbol{n})\ge 0. \end{align*} Therefore, the Bochner's theorem (see, e.g.,~\cite[Section~1.4.3]{Rud62}) implies that $\mathcal{K}$ is a positive definite function on $\mathbb{T}^d$.

nodes.name: Properties of H_j
nodes.statement: The positive definite function $\mathcal{H}_j$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] For all $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$, $\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}})$. \item[(2)] The support of $\mathcal{H}_j$ is contained in $\overline{B}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})$. \item[(3)] The sum of $\mathcal{H}_j$ is of log-type, that is, \[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\log_+\frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{z}\|}+g_0(\|\boldsymbol{z}\|),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus\{\boldsymbol{1}\}. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.statement_short: H_j is symmetric, supported in the ball of radius 2^{-j} around 1, and the H_j sum to a log-correlated kernel.
conclusions: For all $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$, $\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}})$.
The support of $\mathcal{H}_j$ is contained in $\overline{B}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})$.
The sum of $\mathcal{H}_j$ is of log-type
nodes.label: lemma:properties-Hj

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: (1) For $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\in \mathbb{T}^d$ with $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in (-1/2,1/2)^d$, we have \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t})=\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(2^j u\boldsymbol{t})}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(2^j u(-\boldsymbol{t}))}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\mathcal{L}_j(-\boldsymbol{t})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}). \] The third equality holds since $\Phi$ is isotropic. If $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(-1/2),e(-1/2),\ldots,e(-1/2))=(-1,-1,\ldots,-1)$, then $\boldsymbol{z}=\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}$. In this case, $\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}})$ holds automatically. Therefore, we have shown that $\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}})$ for all $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$. (2) For $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$ with $d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{1})>2^{-j}$, the canonical representation $(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)$ of $\boldsymbol{z}$ in $[-1/2,1/2)$ satisfies \[ \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^d |t_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}> 2^{-j}. \] Combining with the fact that $\operatorname{supp} \mathcal{L}_j\subset \overline{B}(\boldsymbol{0},2^{-j})$, we have \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{L}_j(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)=0. \] Therefore, the support of $\mathcal{H}_j$ lies in $\overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})$. (3) Let $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus\{\boldsymbol{1}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in [-1/2,1/2)^d$. Then \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{L}_j(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)=\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t}). \] Therefore, by \eqref{eq:property-Lj}, we have \[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t})=\log_+ \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{t}\|}+g_0(|\boldsymbol{t}|)=\log_+ \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{z}\|}+g_0(\|\boldsymbol{z}\|). \] This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.statement_short: Check each property directly from the definition of L_j: isotropy of Phi, support of L_j, and the log-sum of L_j.

nodes.name: (1) Symmetry from isotropy of Phi
nodes.statement: (1) For $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\in \mathbb{T}^d$ with $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in (-1/2,1/2)^d$, we have \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t})=\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(2^j u\boldsymbol{t})}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(2^j u(-\boldsymbol{t}))}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\mathcal{L}_j(-\boldsymbol{t})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}). \] The third equality holds since $\Phi$ is isotropic. If $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(-1/2),e(-1/2),\ldots,e(-1/2))=(-1,-1,\ldots,-1)$, then $\boldsymbol{z}=\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}$. In this case, $\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}})$ holds automatically. Therefore, we have shown that $\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{H}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}})$ for all $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: (2) Support from support of L_j
nodes.statement: (2) For $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d$ with $d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{1})>2^{-j}$, the canonical representation $(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)$ of $\boldsymbol{z}$ in $[-1/2,1/2)$ satisfies \[ \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^d |t_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}> 2^{-j}. \] Combining with the fact that $\operatorname{supp} \mathcal{L}_j\subset \overline{B}(\boldsymbol{0},2^{-j})$, we have \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{L}_j(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)=0. \] Therefore, the support of $\mathcal{H}_j$ lies in $\overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: (3) Log-sum from the L_j identity
nodes.statement: (3) Let $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus\{\boldsymbol{1}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in [-1/2,1/2)^d$. Then \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{L}_j(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)=\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t}). \] Therefore, by \eqref{eq:property-Lj}, we have \[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t})=\log_+ \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{t}\|}+g_0(|\boldsymbol{t}|)=\log_+ \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{z}\|}+g_0(\|\boldsymbol{z}\|). \] This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Moments of a Gaussian random variable
nodes.statement: If $\xi$ is a Gaussian random variable, then for any $0<p<\infty$, we have \[ \big(\mathbb{E}[|\xi|^p]\big)^{1/p}=\sqrt{2}\cdot \bigg(\frac{\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)^{1/p}\cdot \big(\mathbb{E}[|\xi|^2]\big)^{1/2}. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.5
nodes.statement: Let $\eta_j$ be a centered Gaussian process with kernel function $\mathcal{H}_j$. By Kolmogorov's continuity theorem (see, e.g.,~\cite[Chapter~4, Theorem~4.23]{Kal21}), it is sufficient to verify that \[ \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^{2d}]\le C(j,d,C_\Phi) (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^{2d},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d, \] where $C(j,d,C_\Phi)$ is a constant depending on $j$, $d$ and $C_\Phi$. For $\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d$, let $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in [-1/2,1/2)^d$, such that $\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]=2\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{1})-2\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}})=2\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{0})-2\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t}). \end{align*} By the definition of $\mathcal{L}_j$ and \eqref{eq:properties-Phi}, we have \[ \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]=2\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(\boldsymbol{0})-\Phi(2^ju\boldsymbol{t})}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\le 2C_\Phi 2^{2j}\|\boldsymbol{t}\|^2\int_1^2 u\,\mathrm{d}u=3C_\Phi 2^{2j}\cdot (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^2. \] Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lp-Gaussian-equiv}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^{2d}]&= 2^d\cdot \bigg(\frac{\Gamma((2d+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot \bigg(\mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]\bigg)^d\\ &\le C_\Phi^d\cdot 6^d\cdot \bigg(\frac{\Gamma((2d+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot 2^{2jd}\cdot (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^{2d}. \end{align*} This shows that $\eta_j$ admits a continuous version denoted by $\xi_j$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.statement_short: Kolmogorov continuity criterion: bound increments of eta_j in L^2 via C_Phi, then lift to L^{2d} with Gaussian moments.

nodes.name: Reduce to Kolmogorov's increment bound
nodes.statement: Let $\eta_j$ be a centered Gaussian process with kernel function $\mathcal{H}_j$. By Kolmogorov's continuity theorem (see, e.g.,~\cite[Chapter~4, Theorem~4.23]{Kal21}), it is sufficient to verify that \[ \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^{2d}]\le C(j,d,C_\Phi) (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^{2d},\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d, \] where $C(j,d,C_\Phi)$ is a constant depending on $j$, $d$ and $C_\Phi$.

nodes.name: Express L^2 increment through L_j
nodes.statement: For $\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d$, let $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)\in [-1/2,1/2)^d$, such that $\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]=2\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{1})-2\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}})=2\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{0})-2\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{t}). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Bound L^2 increment using C_Phi
nodes.statement: By the definition of $\mathcal{L}_j$ and \eqref{eq:properties-Phi}, we have \[ \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]=2\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(\boldsymbol{0})-\Phi(2^ju\boldsymbol{t})}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\le 2C_\Phi 2^{2j}\|\boldsymbol{t}\|^2\int_1^2 u\,\mathrm{d}u=3C_\Phi 2^{2j}\cdot (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^2. \]
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Lift to 2d-th moment by Gaussian moments
nodes.statement: Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lp-Gaussian-equiv}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^{2d}]&= 2^d\cdot \bigg(\frac{\Gamma((2d+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot \bigg(\mathbb{E}[|\eta_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\eta_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]\bigg)^d\\ &\le C_\Phi^d\cdot 6^d\cdot \bigg(\frac{\Gamma((2d+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot 2^{2jd}\cdot (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^{2d}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Independence of the processes xi_j
nodes.statement: We always assume that $\{\xi_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus \{0\}}$ are independent.

nodes.name: Isotropic mollifier profile Q
nodes.statement: Let $Q\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be a non-negative isotropic function with $\operatorname{supp} Q\subset \overline{B}(\boldsymbol{0},1)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Rescaled mollifiers Q_j and scales epsilon_j
nodes.statement: For each $j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$, define \[ Q_j(\boldsymbol{t})=\varepsilon_j^{-d}Q\bigg(\frac{\boldsymbol{t}}{\varepsilon_j}\bigg),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{t}\in \mathbb{R}^d,\quad \text{where}~\varepsilon_j\coloneq j^{-2}2^{-j}. \]
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Choice of the mollification scale epsilon_j
nodes.statement: The specific decay rate of $\varepsilon_j$ is carefully chosen to satisfy two distinct requirements in the subsequent proofs. \begin{itemize} \item \textit{Exponential component.} The term $2^{-j}$ is chosen to match the natural scale of the $j$-th process. \item \textit{Polynomial component.} The term $j^{-2}$ ensures a sufficiently rapid mollification. This allows the resulting smooth process to closely approximate the original one, a fact that is made precise in Lemma~\ref{lemma:convergence-difference}. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.statement_short: 2^{-j} matches the natural scale; the extra j^{-2} makes the mollified process close to the original (Lemma 3.7).

nodes.name: Torus mollifier P_j
nodes.statement: The mollifier $P_j \in C^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)$ is defined by $P_j(\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{t})) \coloneqq Q_j(\boldsymbol{t})$ for all $\boldsymbol{t} \in [-1/2, 1/2)^d$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Ball B_j containing supp P_j
nodes.statement: For convenience, we denote this ball by $\mathcal{B}_j$, defined as \begin{equation} \mathcal{B}_j \coloneqq \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\mathbf{1}, j^{-2}2^{-j}). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Definition of B_j
nodes.statement: \mathcal{B}_j \coloneqq \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\mathbf{1}, j^{-2}2^{-j}).
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.label: eq:def-mathcalBj

nodes.name: Support of P_j
nodes.statement: \operatorname{supp} P_j \subset \mathcal{B}_j.

nodes.label: eq:supp-Pj

nodes.name: Mollified processes psi_j = P_j * xi_j
nodes.statement: Define \[ \psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq (P_j*\xi_j)(\boldsymbol{z})=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} P_j(\boldsymbol{w})\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}})\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \]
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Computation of the covariance of psi_j
nodes.statement: We now compute the covariance kernel of $\psi_j$, which we denote by $K_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1, \boldsymbol{z}_2)$: \begin{align*} K_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1,\boldsymbol{z}_2)\coloneq \mathbb{E}[\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1)\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_2)]&=\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_2)\mathbb{E}\big[\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_1)\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_2\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\big]\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_2)\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2). \end{align*} We adopt the standard notationin in harmonic analysis: \[ \widetilde{P}_j(\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq P_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \] Then we can rewrite the covariance function as \begin{align*} \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1,\boldsymbol{z}_2)&=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\widetilde{P}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\boldsymbol{w}_2\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_1)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \widetilde{P}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)(\mathcal{H}_j*P_j)(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\cdot \boldsymbol{w}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \widetilde{P}_j(\boldsymbol{w}_2)(\mathcal{H}_j*P_j)(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=((\mathcal{H}_j*P_j)*\widetilde{P}_j)(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.statement_short: Expand the covariance of P_j*xi_j and rewrite the double integral as H_j*P_j*tilde P_j.

nodes.name: Write the covariance as a double integral against H_j
nodes.statement: We now compute the covariance kernel of $\psi_j$, which we denote by $K_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1, \boldsymbol{z}_2)$: \begin{align*} K_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1,\boldsymbol{z}_2)\coloneq \mathbb{E}[\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1)\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_2)]&=\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_2)\mathbb{E}\big[\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_1)\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z}_2\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\big]\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_2)\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1
nodes.statement_short: Write the covariance as a double integral against H_j

nodes.name: Introduce reflected mollifier tilde P_j
nodes.statement: We adopt the standard notationin in harmonic analysis: \[ \widetilde{P}_j(\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq P_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \]
nodes.section: 3.1 Construction of smooth processes in Proposition~3.1

nodes.name: Rewrite as iterated convolution
nodes.statement: Then we can rewrite the covariance function as \begin{align*} \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1,\boldsymbol{z}_2)&=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\widetilde{P}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\boldsymbol{w}_2\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_1)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \widetilde{P}_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)(\mathcal{H}_j*P_j)(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\cdot \boldsymbol{w}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} \widetilde{P}_j(\boldsymbol{w}_2)(\mathcal{H}_j*P_j)(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2\cdot \bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=((\mathcal{H}_j*P_j)*\widetilde{P}_j)(\boldsymbol{z}_1\bar{\boldsymbol{z}}_2). \end{align*}

nodes.label: eq:def-Kj

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: We need to verify the properties (P0)--(P4) in Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-decomposition-log-correlated-field} for the process $(\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z}))_{\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d}$. \medskip {\flushleft \bf Verification of (P0).} Since $\{\eta_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}}$ are required to be independent, it follows that the mollified processes $\{\psi_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}}$ are independent as well. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:mollification-Gaussian-process}, we know that the process $\psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})$ has $C^\infty$-path almost surely for each $j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$. Hence (P0) in Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-decomposition-log-correlated-field} is satisfied. \medskip {\flushleft \bf Verification of (P1).} To verify (P1), we should analyze the support of the function $\mathcal{K}_j$, which was derived in \S\ref{ssec:construc-smooth-decom} as $\mathcal{K}_{j}=\mathcal{H}_{j}*(P_{j}*\widetilde{P}_{j})$. \begin{lemma} Let $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)$. Then $\operatorname{supp}(f*g)\subset (\operatorname{supp} f)\cdot (\operatorname{supp} g)$, where \[ (\operatorname{supp} f)\cdot (\operatorname{supp} g)\coloneq \{\boldsymbol{w}_1\cdot \boldsymbol{w}_2:\boldsymbol{w}_1\in \operatorname{supp} f,\boldsymbol{w}_2\in \operatorname{supp} g\}. \] \end{lemma} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:properties-Hj}, we have $\operatorname{supp} \mathcal{H}_j\subset \overline{B}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})$. Since $\operatorname{supp} P_j\subset \mathcal{B}_j$, where $\mathcal{B}_j=\overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},j^{-2}2^{-j})$ as we define in \eqref{eq:def-mathcalBj}, we have \[ \operatorname{supp} \mathcal{K}_j=\operatorname{supp} (\mathcal{H}_j*P_j*\widetilde{P}_j)\subset \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})\cdot \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},j^{-2}2^{-j})\cdot \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},j^{-2}2^{-j}). \] By the triangle inequality, we have \[ \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})\cdot \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},j^{-2}2^{-j})\cdot \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},j^{-2}2^{-j})\subset \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},(1+2j^{-2})2^{-j})\subset \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},3\cdot 2^{-j}). \] Hence $\operatorname{supp} \mathcal{K}_j\subset \overline{B}_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{1},3\cdot2^{-j})$ for all $j\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$. Note that \[ \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \] The continuity of $\mathcal{K}_j$ implies that, if $d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})\ge 3\cdot2^{-j}$, then $\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=0$. This proves (P1). \medskip {\flushleft \bf Verification of (P2). } The following lemma is the key to verifying (P2) and (P3), as it establishes a summable error bound between the kernels $\mathcal{K}_j$ and $\mathcal{H}_j$, ensuring the properties of their sum are preserved. \begin{lemma} Let $\mathcal{H}_j$ and $\mathcal{K}_j$ be the positive definite functions defined in \eqref{eq:def-Hj} and \eqref{eq:def-Kj}. Then we have \[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \|\mathcal{K}_j-\mathcal{H}_j\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}<\infty. \] \end{lemma} \begin{lemma} Let $\mathcal{H}_j$ be the kernel function in \eqref{eq:def-Hj}. Then \[ |\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{w})|\le C 2^jd_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d, \] where $C$ is a constant independent of $j$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $\xi_j$ be the Gaussian process in Corollary~\ref{corollary:original-process} and $\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d$. Then, \[ |\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{w})|=|\mathbb{E}[\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})\xi_j(\boldsymbol{1})]-\mathbb{E}[\xi_j(\boldsymbol{w})\xi_j(\boldsymbol{1})]|= |\mathbb{E}[\xi_j(\boldsymbol{1})(\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\xi_j(\boldsymbol{w}))]|. \] By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have \[ |\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{w})|\le (\mathbb{E}[|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{1})|^2])^{1/2}\cdot (\mathbb{E}[|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\xi_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2])^{1/2}. \] Following the same line in the proof of Proposition~\ref{corollary:original-process}, we have \[ \mathbb{E}[|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\xi_j(\boldsymbol{w})|^2]\le 3C_\Phi 2^{2j}\cdot (d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}))^2. \] Therefore, \[ |\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{w})|\le (\log 2)^{1/2}\cdot (3C_\Phi )^{1/2}\cdot 2^j d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}). \] This proves the lemma. \end{proof} \begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:convergence-difference}] Fix $\boldsymbol{z}=(e(t_1),e(t_2),\ldots,e(t_d))\in \mathbb{T}^d$. By definition, \begin{align*} \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=(\mathcal{H}_j*P_j*\widetilde{P_j})(\boldsymbol{z})=\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\cdot\overline{\boldsymbol{w}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2})\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2). \end{align*} Since $\operatorname{supp} P_j\subset \mathcal{B}_j$, \begin{align*} \big|\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})\big|&=\bigg|\iint_{\mathbb{T}^d\times \mathbb{T}^d} P(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)(\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\cdot\overline{\boldsymbol{w}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}))\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\bigg|\\ &\le \iint_{\mathcal{B}_j\times \mathcal{B}_j}P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)|\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\cdot\overline{\boldsymbol{w}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})|\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2). \end{align*} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lipschitz-continuity-kernel}, we have \begin{align*} |\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\cdot \overline{\boldsymbol{w}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})|&\le C2^j d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z}\cdot \overline{\boldsymbol{w}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2},\boldsymbol{z})\\ &=C2^jd_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{w}_1\boldsymbol{w}_2,\boldsymbol{1}) \\ & \le C2^j\cdot (2j^{-2}2^{-j})=2Cj^{-2}. \end{align*} Therefore, \begin{align*} |\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z})-\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})|&\le 2Cj^{-2}\cdot \iint_{\mathcal{B}_j\times \mathcal{B}_j} P_j(\boldsymbol{w}_1)P_j(\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}_2)\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_1)\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_2)\\ &=2Cj^{-2}\cdot \iint_{[-1/2,1/2)^d\times [-1/2,1/2)^d} Q_j(\boldsymbol{x})Q_j(-\boldsymbol{y})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{y}\\ &=2Cj^{-2}\cdot \bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} Q_j(\boldsymbol{x})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}\bigg)^2=2Cj^{-2}. \end{align*} Since the choice of $\boldsymbol{z}$ is arbitrary, we have \[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \|\mathcal{K}_j-\mathcal{H}_j\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}\le 2C\cdot \sum_{j=1}^\infty j^{-2}<\infty. \] This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:convergence-difference}. \end{proof} Define \[ g_1(\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq \sum_{j=1}^\infty (\mathcal{K}_j-\mathcal{H}_j)(\boldsymbol{z}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \] Then, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:convergence-difference}, the function $g_1$ is continuous on $\mathbb{T}^d$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:properties-Hj}, we have \[ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})=\log \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d}}+g_0(\|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus\{\boldsymbol{1}\}, \] where $g_0\in C^1([0,\sqrt{d}])$. Let $g(\boldsymbol{z})\coloneq g_1(\boldsymbol{z})+g_0(\|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d})$, then $g$ is continuous on $\mathbb{T}^d$. Thus, for all $\boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus\{\boldsymbol{1}\}$, we have \begin{align*} \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z})&=\sum_{j=1}^\infty (\mathcal{K}_j-\mathcal{H}_j)(\boldsymbol{z})+\sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{z})\\ &=g_1(\boldsymbol{z})+\log_+ \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d}}+g_0(\|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d})\\ &=\log_+ \frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{z}\|_{\mathbb{T}^d}}+g(\boldsymbol{z}). \end{align*} This completes the verification of (P2). \medskip {\flushleft \bf Verification of (P3). } By definition of $\mathcal{H}_j$ and \eqref{eq:properties-Phi}, we have \[ \mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{1})=\mathcal{L}_j(\boldsymbol{0})=\int_1^2 \frac{\Phi(\boldsymbol{0})}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\log 2. \] Since $\lim_{j\to \infty}\|\mathcal{K}_j-\mathcal{H}_j\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}=0$, we obtain the convergence at $\boldsymbol{1}$, that is, \[ \lim_{j\to \infty}\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{1})=\lim_{j\to \infty}\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{1})=\log 2. \] \medskip {\flushleft \bf Verification of (P4). } Inspired by \eqref{eq:diff-convolution} in Lemma~\ref{lemma:convolution-deterministic}, it is necessary to control the $L^\infty$-norm of derivatives of $P_j$. \begin{lemma} For any multi-index $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ with $|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|\le d$ and $j\ge 1$, we have \[ \|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P_j(\boldsymbol{z})\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}\le j^{2(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}2^{j(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}\|Q\|_{C^d(\mathbb{R}^d)}. \] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} By the definition of $P_j$, we have \[ D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P_j(\boldsymbol{z})=j^{2d}2^{jd}D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} Q_j(\boldsymbol{t}), \] where $\boldsymbol{t}=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_d)$ is the canonical representation of $\boldsymbol{z}$ in $[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and $\varepsilon_j=j^{-2}2^{-j}$. By the chain rule, we have \[ \bigg(\partial^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} Q\bigg(\frac{\cdot}{\varepsilon_j}\bigg)\bigg)(\boldsymbol{t})=\varepsilon_j^{-|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|}(\partial^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} Q)\bigg(\frac{\boldsymbol{t}}{\varepsilon_j}\bigg)=j^{2|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|}2^{j|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|}(\partial^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} Q)\bigg(\frac{\boldsymbol{t}}{\varepsilon_j}\bigg). \] Therefore, \[ \|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P_j(\boldsymbol{z})\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}=j^{2(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}2^{j(\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}\|\partial^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} Q\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le j^{2(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}2^{j(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}\cdot\|Q\|_{C^d(\mathbb{R}^d)}. \] This proves the lemma. \end{proof} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:mollification-Gaussian-process}, we know \[ (D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \psi_j)(\boldsymbol{z})=D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} (P_j*\xi_j)(\boldsymbol{z})=((D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P_j)*\xi_j)(\boldsymbol{z}). \] Recalling that $\operatorname{supp} P_j\subset \mathcal{B}_j$ in \eqref{eq:supp-Pj}, we have \begin{align*} |D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|&\le \int_{\mathcal{B}_j}\|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} P_j\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^d)}\cdot |\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\\ &\le \|Q\|_{C^d(\mathbb{R}^d)}\cdot j^{2(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}2^{j(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)}\cdot \int_{\mathcal{B}_j}|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}). \end{align*} Let $0<p<\infty$. The $p$-moment of $D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\psi_j$ can be estimated by \[ \mathbb{E}[|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^p]\le \|Q\|_{C^d(\mathbb{R}^d)}^p\cdot j^{2(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)p}2^{j(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|+d)p}\cdot \mathbb{E}\bigg[\bigg|\int_{\mathcal{B}_j}|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\bigg|^p\bigg]. \] By Minkowski's inequality and Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lp-Gaussian-equiv}, we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\bigg[\bigg|\int_{\mathcal{B}_j}|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\bigg|^p\bigg]&\le \bigg\{\int_{\mathcal{B}_j}\big(\mathbb{E}[|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^p]\big)^{1/p}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\bigg\}^p\\ &=2^{p/2}\bigg(\frac{\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot \bigg\{\int_{\mathcal{B}_j}\big(\mathbb{E}[|\xi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^2]\big)^{1/2}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\bigg\}^p\\ &=2^{p/2}\bigg(\frac{\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot \bigg\{\int_{\mathcal{B}_j}\big(\mathcal{H}_j(\boldsymbol{1})\big)^{1/2}\,\boldsymbol{m}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z})\bigg\}^p\\ &=(2\log 2)^{p/2}\bigg(\frac{\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot (\Omega_d j^{-2d}2^{-jd})^p, \end{align*} where $\Omega_d$ is the volume of unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Denote \[ \Theta(p)=\max\bigg\{1,\|Q\|_{C^d(\mathbb{R}^d)}^p\cdot (2\log 2)^{p/2}\cdot \bigg(\frac{\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigg)\cdot \Omega_d^p\bigg\}. \] Then for all $0<p<\infty$, we have \[ \sup_{j}\sup_{|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|\le d}\sup_{z\in \mathbb{T}^d}\frac{\mathbb{E}\big[|D^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \psi_j(\boldsymbol{z})|^p\big]}{j^{2|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}2^{j|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|p}}\le \Theta(p). \] We claim that $\Theta$ is increasing in $p$. Let $f(p)=\big(\frac{\Gamma((p+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\big)^{1/p}$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lp-Gaussian-equiv} and Lyapunov's inequality, we can see that $f(p)$ is increasing in $p$. It follows that \[ \Theta(p)=\max\Big\{1,\big(\|Q\|_{C^d(\mathbb{R}^d)}\cdot (2\log2)^{1/2}\cdot \Omega_d\cdot f(p)\big)^p\Big\} \] is increasing in $p$ as well. Hence the constructed processes satisfy (P4).
nodes.statement_short: Verify (P0)-(P4) for psi_j=P_j*xi_j: smoothness by mollification, finite range by support of convolution, log-sum and variance by a summable L^infty error K_j-H_j, derivative bounds via derivatives of P_j.

Then $\operatorname{supp}(f*g)\subset (\operatorname{supp} f)\cdot (\operatorname{supp} g)$, where \[ (\operatorname{supp} f)\cdot (\operatorname{supp} g)\coloneq \{\boldsymbol{w}_1\cdot \boldsymbol{w}_2:\boldsymbol{w}_1\in \operatorname{supp} f,\boldsymbol{w}_2\in \operatorname{supp} g\}. \] \end{lemma} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:properties-Hj}, we have $\operatorname{supp} \mathcal{H}_j\subset \overline{B}(\boldsymbol{1},2^{-j})$. Note that \[ \mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z}\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}),\quad \forall \boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{T}^d. \] The continuity of $\mathcal{K}_j$ implies that, if $d_{\mathbb{T}^d}(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})\ge 3\cdot2^{-j}$, then $\mathcal{K}_j(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{w})=0$.
